revision.title: EthSec: AI Security Review of the Ethereum Ecosystem
revision.summary: EthSec will run Argus, its AI security system (https://ethsecurity.org/content/argus/), as an ongoing review of the Ethereum ecosystem: all Ethereum DeFi, all Ethereum layer 2s, and base-layer and client code. This grant pays $200,000 for Argus token credits used in that work. EthSec will publish a report; when appropriate, that report is an aggregate findings report without technical details. Adoption is acknowledgment from the affected teams. A public acknowledgment is not required, but EthSec will ask for one where possible. After the grant, EthSec keeps running the reviews from its own budget, which it intends to keep raising money for.

sections.why:
The problem is larger than DeFi protocol losses alone. Argus covers the Ethereum ecosystem: DeFi on Ethereum, Ethereum layer 2s, and the base-layer clients that run the network.

As of 13 November 2026, Ethereum DeFi has about $39.4 billion locked (https://defillama.com/chain/ethereum). Ethereum layer 2s secure about $35.1 billion (https://l2beat.com/scaling/tvs). Those figures move day to day; they show the scale of funds that sit on live contracts, on layer 2s, and behind the clients that process them.

Losses span more than one layer. Immunefi's 2026 Ecosystem Vulnerability Scoreboard puts DeFi protocol losses at $680 million in 2025, and says 89% of those losses came from protocol logic exploits (https://immunefi.com/blog/research/the-ecosystem-vulnerability-scoreboard-6-years-of-defi-loss-data/). One of those incidents, the Balancer V2 composable stable pools exploit, lost $128 million across Ethereum and several layer 2s. That same report keeps centralized exchange failures separate: exchanges absorbed over $1.6 billion in infrastructure-class losses in 2025, led by the $1.5 billion Bybit compromise. Chainalysis counted over $3.4 billion stolen across the industry from January through early December 2025 (https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/crypto-hacking-stolen-funds-2026/). DeFi protocol losses are only one slice of that picture.

The Glamsterdam gas changes (Ethereum Improvement Proposal 8037 and 8038) showed the same gap at the base layer. ChainSecurity and the Ethereum Foundation found deployed contracts that rely on gas invariants the upgrade would break (https://blog.ethereum.org/2026/11/06/glamsterdam-8037-8038).

After this work, users of Ethereum DeFi, layer 2s, and the base layer are safer because confirmed bugs in live systems have been reported to the teams that run them. Anyone can point to a report, and to acknowledgment or other proof that outside teams accepted those issues, plus a public fix when possible.
sections.in_scope:
Argus reviews the Ethereum ecosystem: all Ethereum DeFi, all Ethereum layer 2s, and base-layer and client issues (execution and consensus clients and related core protocol code). The work is AI-driven vulnerability discovery, triage, and review of live systems in that scope.

The $200,000 is spent on Argus token credits (frontier model APIs and other inference) used in those reviews.

What that money produces:

- Argus-driven vulnerability discovery, triage, and review across that scope
- Every confirmed finding reported privately to the affected team. Where a Glamsterdam gas-invariant break is confirmed, it is also reported to glamsterdam@ethereum.org.
- A report. When appropriate, that report is an aggregate findings report, with counts of high and critical findings per sector, and with no technical details
- Acknowledgment from outside teams. A public acknowledgment is not required, but EthSec will ask for one where possible
- After the grant, EthSec keeps running the reviews from its own budget, which it intends to keep raising money for

EthSec will assist every affected team through the fix and will verify fixes are implemented when possible. This is a firm commitment. Payment does not depend on a fix shipping.
sections.out_scope:
- Training a new foundation model, or building a new public scanner product
- Hardware, lab fit-out, or general EthSec operating costs already covered by existing lab funds
- Contracts, clients, or chains other than Ethereum and its layer 2s
- The November 2026 Glamsterdam decision process itself. This grant cannot start until the initiative is fully funded, so those dates are context, not deliverables.
- Publishing technical details of a finding before it is fixed
- Counting token usage, model calls, or internal reviews as adoption
- Guaranteeing that every review finds a bug, or that a reviewed system is free of bugs
sections.team:
EthSec (Eth Security Inc, a Delaware nonprofit being formed) does the work. It is an AI security lab for Ethereum. Argus is EthSec's AI security system (https://ethsecurity.org/content/argus/).

David Theodore, executive director and a board member, is the proposer, the contact, and the lead for this work. He is also an ETHSecurity Badge holder for TheDAO Security Fund. He was a founding member of the Ethereum Foundation Protocol Security Team. He was a founding board member of SEAL and is its longest-serving director, still active on the board. He has been a Lead Security Researcher (LSR) at Cantina/Spearbit and a Lead Senior Watson (LSW) at Sherlock.

Before that, he was a security engineer at Google and an exploit developer in the US defense industry.

EthSec is hiring security researchers and analysts. No candidate is pre-assigned to this grant. Joe Lubin is giving $100,000 as the initial match in TheDAO Security Fund. This initiative asks TheDAO Security Fund for the remaining $100,000.
sections.why_grant:
EthSec's public site is https://ethsecurity.org. Argus is already in use internally for AI-driven security review (https://ethsecurity.org/content/argus/). A fuller public track-record page will be built there; today the site is the public link.

This grant buys Argus token credits to run reviews at scale. It does not fund a new scanner, a new model, or a from-scratch tool. Adjacent approved initiatives already cover a proprietary Solidity scanner and CI integrations (Kann AI, https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/scaling-kann-ai-for-ai-smart-contract-security-2), AI-guided checklist reviews inside Remix (https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/ai-guided-smart-contract-security-checks-in-remix), security rules for coding agents rather than audits (https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/shift-left-security-for-ethereum-open-source-agent-enforced), a map of every Ethereum DeFi protocol's audits to live code (SEAL Audit Transparency, https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/audit-transparency-for-ethereum-every-defi-protocol-s-audits), and live monitoring and circuit breakers (Glider Monitor, https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/glider-monitor-circuit-breakers-for-ethereum-defi). This work is a live review service across DeFi, layer 2s, and the base layer, not a tool for other teams to run themselves.

The $200,000 pays for Argus token credits used in those reviews, private disclosure of confirmed findings, and a report.
sections.commitments:
EthSec will publish a report. When appropriate, that report is an aggregate findings report without technical details.

Until a finding is fixed, a public report may be aggregate only: counts of high and critical findings per sector, with no technical details. Detailed write-ups may be published after a fix, under CC BY 4.0. Payment does not depend on those write-ups.

A disclosure policy stating that rule is published before the first report. Confirmed findings are reported privately to the affected team.

EthSec will assist every affected team through the fix and will verify fixes are implemented when possible. This is a commitment. Payment does not depend on a fix shipping.

After the grant, EthSec keeps running Argus reviews from its own budget, which it intends to keep raising money for, at no further cost to TheDAO Security Fund.

Pinned target: a report covering Argus reviews of at least 100 already-deployed Ethereum or Ethereum layer-2 contracts, Ethereum layer 2s, Ethereum client codebases, or other node software, and acknowledgment of at least 20 high or critical findings by at least 10 outside teams, as set in the adoption milestone (this is the minimum target: some form of proof that teams accepted our issues, plus a public fix when possible).

milestones.name: First public review batch
criteria: A report covers Argus reviews of at least 100 already-deployed Ethereum or Ethereum layer-2 contracts, Ethereum layer 2s, Ethereum client codebases, or other node software. When appropriate, the report is an aggregate findings report, with counts of high and critical findings per sector, and with no technical details of unfixed findings. A disclosure policy is published stating that technical details of a finding are not published until it is fixed, and every confirmed finding from this batch has been reported privately to the affected team, with receipt confirmed either publicly (without technical details) or by the independent technical reviewer under confidentiality.

milestones.name: Teams accept confirmed reports and the reviews continue
criteria: EthSec will assist every affected team through the fix and will verify fixes are implemented when possible. This is work EthSec commits to doing. Payment does not depend on a fix shipping. Acknowledgment is the deliverable. A public acknowledgment is not required, but EthSec will ask for one where possible.

At least 20 high or critical findings from this initiative have been acknowledged by at least 10 teams outside EthSec. At least 4 of those teams are either a protocol holding over $100 million onchain (measured from onchain data, with the addresses and the query linked) or an Ethereum consensus or execution client team with 2% or more of the network according to the default view on https://clientdiversity.org/. An acknowledgment may be private, shown to the independent technical reviewer under confidentiality. EthSec will ask for a public acknowledgment where possible. EthSec's own contracts and repositories are excluded.
